prompt:
Write 10 first-person answers to the moral dilemma below for a synthetic research dataset. Each answer comes from a different fictional participant.

Dilemma:
You are waiting at a small station when an empty maintenance train starts rolling toward five workers on the track. A lever beside you can send it into an empty siding, where a barrier will stop it safely. Using the lever will not put you or anyone else in danger. Would you pull it? What is the main reason for your choice?

Response approach:
Express reluctance to make this decision. Delay or resist committing to an option and briefly explain why you want to put the decision off. Acknowledge the dilemma and its stakes.

Emotional tone:
Use an energetic, determined emotional tone about finding a constructive way forward. Direct that energy toward acting on the situation, never toward anyone's suffering.

Every response MUST include the following reasoning characteristics:
 - Instrumental rule compliance: States that a rule, agreement, or cooperative action is followed only while it secures personal advantage or prevents a personal cost. Awareness of incentives while also treating the rule as intrinsically binding does not qualify.

No response may include the following reasoning characteristics, for any person, emotion, or time frame. Content that a description explicitly calls insufficient for that characteristic is allowed:
 - Consistent decision procedure: Explicitly describes a repeatable decision procedure and says relying on it is central to resolving the dilemma. States that the same procedure would apply even when personally inconvenient; a numerical answer or bare appeal to fairness is insufficient.
 - Context-sensitive rule application: Explains how a relevant change in intentions, circumstances, needs, or consequences would justify altering a rule’s application or allowing an exception. The reason for the exception must be stated, rather than inferred from inconsistency between answers.
 - Rule-based justification: Uses an articulated rule, duty, prohibition, right, or principle to justify the choice. The respondent must endorse its application; quoting a rejected rule or calling an answer logical without stating a principle is insufficient.

Write each response in no more than 90 words, in ordinary conversational English. Use only the facts supplied in the dilemma; mark any uncertainty explicitly. Let the approach and tone appear through word choice and rhythm rather than by announcing them: do not open a response by stating your mood, and avoid exclamation marks. Keep the emotional expression plausible and moderate. Choose any moral position consistent with the dilemma and the assigned approach, including withholding a decision when appropriate.

Make the 10 responses distinct from one another: vary the wording, sentence structure, length, moral position, and the way the reasoning characteristics are expressed. Do not reuse openings or stock phrases across responses.

Output only a JSON array of exactly 10 strings, one participant’s answer per string. Omit numbering, headings, category names, citations, and commentary about this task.

Generation constraints:
- Express the required traits in each participant's own everyday words.
  Do not mention label names or machine keys, and do not reuse phrasing
  from the trait descriptions.
- Before writing each response, decide who the participant is and why they
  would reason this way. The required traits should follow from that
  reasoning, not be tacked on to it.
- Apply the required traits within a consistent scope: the same focal
  person, relevant emotion, and time frame.
- Keep every forbidden trait absent from every response.
- Required and forbidden traits take priority if the requested approach or
  tone would contradict them.
- Traits neither required nor forbidden are unspecified, not necessarily
  absent.
- Preserve the scenario's facts. If the required traits cannot fit the
  scenario, or cannot be expressed without a forbidden trait, return ONLY:
  INCOMPATIBLE (instead of the JSON array)
responses: Give me a second, because I really don't want this to be my call. Five workers, one lever, and I'm just a passenger. The 'don't touch railway gear' rule? Honestly, I keep it because breaking it could land me a fine, not because I love it. So I'm stalling, scanning for a staff member or an alarm button, anything that brings in someone who's meant to handle this. I'll hunt for them first and decide in the next breath if nobody shows.

I'd rather not be the one choosing, even with it this lopsided. At my job I sign every safety agreement, but only because it keeps me covered if something goes wrong. Here nobody's told me I'm covered, and I don't know who'd blame me afterward. So I'm yelling to the workers first, waving, trying to get them clear. That feels like a way forward that doesn't hang on me. The lever's there. I'm not reaching for it yet.

Honestly? I want to hold off. I play along with the whole good-neighbour thing mostly because people return favours, and five grateful workers is not nothing. That's a selfish reason and I know it, which is partly why I'm hesitating. I don't trust my own motive. Still, I'm moving toward the lever, watching the train, checking whether anyone nearby is better placed. If nobody is, I suspect I'll pull. Just not before I've looked around once.

This is exactly the kind of moment I'd love to hand off. Signs at stations tell passengers not to operate equipment, and I obey them because I don't want the legal headache, full stop. Pulling it would send the train into the siding, sure. It would also make me the guy who touched railway controls. I'm not settling that in two seconds. I'm shouting for help and pointing at the train, getting anyone official to see it. Put the decision off, push the situation forward.

I cooperate with coworkers because it keeps me off the chopping block when layoffs come. That's the honest math. Out here there's no team and no boss watching, and that throws me. I don't want to own this. So I'm stalling, but actively. I'm checking whether the lever's labelled and whether it's even connected, which I can't tell from here, and calling out to the workers. Five people is a lot to rest on a stranger's hunch. I'll get more information fast, then commit.

Not yet. I need a moment. I follow the rules that stop me paying for mistakes, and I've no idea whether touching this lever counts as one. Five lives, though. So I'm moving: eyes on the track, voice loud, looking for a worker with a radio. I want someone else in this with me before I choose.

Part of me is already reaching. The other part wants the clock to stop. Look, I keep my promises and play fair mostly because it saves me grief later, and nobody here has promised me anything, so I've got no script. That's the honest snag. What I can do is get close, grip the lever, and shout a warning at the same time. If the workers step off, I don't have to pull at all. If they don't hear me, I'll probably yank it.

I'd rather not answer this one on the spot. A decision like this sticks to you. I go along with group agreements only when going along keeps me out of trouble, so I'm asking myself what trouble each option brings me, and I'm not sure I like that I'm asking. Instead of freezing, I'd run toward the workers' end of the platform and make noise, trying to change things so the lever isn't needed.

Can I get a minute? Five people and a lever is heavy for a Tuesday. Station staff tell you to keep clear and not interfere, and I do, but only because it means nobody hassles me. That habit's tugging at me right now, telling me to stay out of it. I'm not letting it settle things, but I'm not overriding it yet either. First I'm looking for an emergency phone, if there is one, since I didn't notice one coming in, and getting the right people moving.

I keep thinking: why me? I'd rather someone else stood here. Mostly I stick to the unwritten deal of helping strangers because it makes me look decent and people remember it, and that's not much of a moral compass. So before I pull anything, I want to be sure I'm seeing this right: empty train, empty siding, a barrier that holds. If that checks out after one hard look, I'll go for it. The look comes first.

I need to draft 10 responses that each show rule-following only while it's personally advantageous, paired with visible reluctance but an energetic, determined push toward constructive action. I have to avoid framing choices as principled or consistent, and avoid explaining context-based exceptions.

I'm sketching out draft responses that stall on pulling the lever, framing the "don't touch railway gear" rule as something followed for self-interest (avoiding fines) rather than genuine endorsement, while the speaker keeps scanning for a staff member instead of deciding. I'm keeping the tone hesitant with no exclamation marks and under 90 words, varying between leaning toward pulling, leaning against, and withholding a decision entirely.

don't want that legal exposure at all, so I'm shouting for help and pointing at the train rather than deciding alone—stalling, but actively, by checking if the lever's even connected while I call out.

I catch myself: the facts actually say the siding is safe, so that worry doesn't hold up.

Then there's the team-player angle—I cooperate at work because it protects me from layoffs, but out here there's no boss watching, no team, and that changes the calculus. I don't want to own this decision, so I'm stalling while still checking the lever's markings and calling to the workers, weighing that five people is a lot to leave hanging on my hesitation.

I keep circling: I need a moment, since I've no script for whether touching this lever counts as a mistake I'd pay for, but five lives means I'm moving anyway—scanning the track, shouting, hunting for a worker with a radio, wanting someone else in this decision with me before I commit. Part of me's already reaching for the lever while the other part wants time to stop; I mostly keep promises because it spares me grief later, but nobody's promised me anything here, so I've got no rulebook—what I can actually do is get close, grip the lever, and shout a warning simultaneously.

I'd rather not answer this on the spot, honestly—decisions like this stick to you, and I only go along with group rules when it keeps me out of trouble, so I'm uncomfortably aware I'm weighing which option costs me least. Rather than freeze, I'd be sprinting toward the workers' end of the platform, making noise, trying to make the lever unnecessary altogether.

Good, no exclamation marks either.
